citeAs: Bisk, Y., Zellers, R., Le Bras, R., Gao, J., and Choi, Y. (2020). PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. AAAI 2020.
creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi (Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Microsoft Research AI, Carnegie Mellon University, University of Washington)
description: PIQA (Physical Interaction: Question Answering) is a benchmark dataset for evaluating physical commonsense reasoning in natural language. It consists of multiple-choice questions where a model must choose the most appropriate solution to a physical goal from two options. The dataset contains over 16,000 training QA pairs with additional development and test sets, inspired by instructables.com and designed to test knowledge of physical properties, affordances, and object manipulation.
name: PIQA
rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotator pay averaged >$15/hr according to both self-reporting on turkerview.com and timing calculations. No further demographic details (nationality, age, gender) are provided.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the dataset. Human performance was calculated by majority vote on development data, achieving 94.9% accuracy. Annotators chosen for human evaluation had achieved 90% on the qualification HIT.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were shown an instructable page as inspiration and asked to provide: (1) a physical goal, (2) a valid solution, and (3) a "trick" — a solution that sounds reasonable but is wrong, often due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. A qualification HIT was run first requiring annotators to achieve >80% accuracy on identifying well-formed vs. underspecified (goal, solution) pairs. Data was collected in batches and validated by other annotators. Users with low agreement were de-qualified. A diff button was provided to highlight differences between solutions. Annotator pay averaged >$15/hr.
rai:dataBiases: Reporting bias was identified as a major concern: when thinking about how to achieve a goal, people are drawn to prototypical solutions and common tools (e.g., forks, knives, hammers), rarely considering the hundreds of other everyday objects. Instructables were used as prompts to flatten the distribution of referenced objects and address this bias. AFLite was applied to remove annotation artifacts that could artificially inflate model performance, as seen in prior NLI benchmarks.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected using Amazon Mechanical Turk (HITs). Annotators were shown instructables.com pages as inspiration and asked to provide a physical goal, a valid solution, and a "trick" (an invalid but plausible-sounding solution). Annotators were seeded with instructables from six categories (costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop), and asked to draw two examples per instructable. Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Instructions from instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions for doing everything from cooking to car repair. In most cases, users provide images or videos detailing each step and a list of tools required. These instructables served as prompts/seeds for human annotators.
rai:dataLimitations: Examples requiring expert-level domain knowledge (e.g., special woodworking terminology) were removed as they fall outside "commonsense." Some model "mistakes" are actually correct answers that required a web search to verify. The dataset was constructed to be adversarial to BERT. Physical commonsense does not have as rich a literature as syntax, making its dimensions challenging to pin down.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The AFLite algorithm was applied to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples. AFLite fine-tunes BERT-Large on 5,000 examples to compute embeddings, then uses an ensemble of linear classifiers trained on random subsets to identify and discard instances whose embeddings are highly indicative of the correct answer label. Goals were tokenized by Spacy, averaging 7.8 words; solutions were tokenized by the GPT BPE tokenizer. Examples were truncated at 150 tokens during model evaluation (affecting 1% of data).
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance AI systems' understanding of physical commonsense, which is critical for building robots that interact with the world and understand natural language. The authors argue that knowledge should be learned from interaction with the world, and PIQA is intended to highlight the gap between language-only learning and true physical understanding.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking progress in physical commonsense understanding for natural language models; evaluating language representations on their knowledge of physical commonsense; probing the inner workings of deep pretrained language models to determine the extent of their physical knowledge; advancing language representations that capture knowledge traditionally only seen or experienced, to enable construction of language models useful beyond NLP (e.g., robotics).
rai:machineAnnotationTools: AFLite algorithm using BERT-Large for embedding computation; Spacy for tokenizing goals; GPT BPE tokenizer for tokenizing solutions and measuring sequence lengths.

evidence.name: we introduce the task of physical commonsense reasoning and a corresponding benchmark dataset Physical Interaction: Question Answering or PIQA
evidence.description: We introduce a new dataset, PIQA, for benchmarking progress in physical commonsense understanding. The underlying task is multiple choice question answering: given a question q and two possible solutions s1, s2, a model or a human must choose the most appropriate solution, of which exactly one is correct.

evidence.isLiveDataset: In total our dataset is comprised of over 16,000 training QA pairs with an additional 2K and 3k held out for development and testing, respectively.
evidence.rai:dataCollection: we seed annotators with instructables drawn from six categories (costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop). We asked that two examples be drawn per instructable to encourage one of them to come later in the process and require precise articulation of pre-conditions. During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: Our dataset is inspired by instructables.com, which provides users with instructions on how to build, craft, bake, or manipulate objects using everyday materials. We asked annotators to provide semantic perturbations or alternative approaches which are otherwise syntactically and topically similar to ensure physical knowledge is targeted.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The instructables website is a crowdsourced collection of instructions for doing everything from cooking to car repair. In most cases, users provide images or videos detailing each step and a list of tools that will be required.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: In addition to this design, we also include a qualiﬁcation HIT which contained well constructed and underspeciﬁed (goal, solution) pairs. Annotators had to successfully (>80%) identify which were well formed to participate in the main HIT. Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness. Users will low agreement were de-qualed.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: In the HIT design the instructable provides inspiration to think out-of-the-box (1 Sock, 3 Products) and annotators are asked for 1. a physical goal, 2. a valid solution, and 3. a trick.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data. Human performance was calculated by a majority vote. Annotators were chosen to participate that achieved 90% on the qualiﬁcation HIT from before.
evidence.rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotator pay averaged >15$/hr according to both self-reporting on turkerview.com and our timing calculations.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The dataset is further cleaned of basic artifacts using the AFLite algorithm introduced in (Sakaguchi et al. 2020; Sap et al. 2019) which is an improvement on adversarial ﬁltering. In practice, we use 5,000 examples from the original dataset to ﬁne-tune BERT-Large for this task and compute the corresponding embeddings of all remaining instances.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: We initially experimented with asking annotators for (task, tool) pairs via unconstrained prompts, but found that reporting bias swamped the dataset. In particular, when thinking about how to achieve a goal, people most often are drawn to prototypical solutions and look for tools in the kitchen (e.g. forks and knives) or the garage (e.g. hammers and drills).
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data. This often meant that correct examples were removed that required expert level knowledge of a domain (e.g. special woodworking terminology) which should not fall under the umbrella of "commonsense."
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: Our goal with PIQA is to provide insight and a benchmark for progress towards language representations that capture knowledge traditionally only seen or experienced, to enable the construction of language models useful beyond the NLP community.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: we hypothesize that modeling physical commonsense knowledge is a major challenge on the road to true AI-completeness, including robots that interact with the world and understand natural language.
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Our goals, as tokenized by Spacy, average 7.8 words and both correct and incorrect solutions average 21.3 words. In total, this leads to over 3.7 million lexical tokens in the training data. Figure 4 shows a plot of the correct and incorrect sequence lengths (as tokenized by the GPT BPE tokenizer)
